newsitem.title: CHINA: China dissident tells leader to avoid dictatorship.
newsitem.headline: China dissident tells leader to avoid dictatorship.

text.p: A Chinese dissident has issued a daring warning to President Jiang Zemin, saying any attempt by the Communist Party chief to revive the title held by former Chairman Mao Zedong would start a slide deep into dictatorship.

Activist Shen Liangqing had sent an open letter to party leaders calling for democratic reform and warning of the perils of personality cults, the former state prosecutor said by telephone from eastern Anhui province on Wednesday.

Rumours have long swirled around China that Jiang hopes to revive the Mao-era title of Communist Party Chairman at a crucial party congress this year, although analysts have said such a move would be unlikely to succeed.
Adoption of the party chairman title by Jiang would mark a slide toward the kind of accumulation of power that allowed Mao to launch the disastrous 1966-76 Cultural Revolution, Shen said.
"The title of Party Chairman destroyed democracy within the party and strengthened the personality cult, central state power and dictatorship," the 35-year-old activist said.

"If there is a party chairman, it will certainly lead to a new personality cult and personal dictatorship," he said in his letter to Jiang, who has taken formal control of China's state, party and army since being named political heir to former paramount leader Deng Xiaoping in 1989.
Economic reform under the leadership of Deng, who died last February, had not been matched by the political changes needed to ensure China's successful modernisation, Shen wrote.
"Under Deng Xiaoping's reform campaign, there has been some progress in the economic sphere, but reform of the political system has always stood still," he wrote.
"If there is a party chairman, people will have reason to believe that the reforms of the revered Deng cannot but wither like a dying flower."
Shen's letter was a daring political gambit in China, where a wave of arrests, detentions and jailings of dissidents last year all but silenced the nation's tiny pro-democracy movement.
The Anhui dissident spent time in detention in the early 1990s, but was released in September 1993 when Beijing was bidding to hold the 2000 Olympics.

He was retroactively sentenced last December to 17 months in prison for counter-revolutionary offences during pro-democracy protests in Anhui in 1989. The sentence included time spent in detention, but he was fired from his job as prosecutor.
In June, Shen wrote to the National People's Congress, China's parliament, demanding a reassessment of the June 4, 1989 suppression by the army of student-led pro-democracy demonstrations in Beijing.
Shen said he hoped the letter to Jiang would not prompt a harsh response from the authorities, but said he had come under tight surveillance after his petition to parliament.
It was vital to show opposition to individual dictatorship, and it would be wrong to imagine that China's political situation could not deteriorate, he said.

"Of course, collective dictatorship is still dictatorship, but I think it is a little better than the dictatorship of an individual," he said. "I oppose the putting of too much power in one person's hands."
